lead: The Clausius–Clapeyron equation gives the slope of a saturation curve from latent heat and volume change. It answers a practical question: water boils at 373 K at 1 atm, so what is its vapour pressure at 350 K? One measured (P, T) pair plus ΔH gives another. A plot of ln P against 1/T gives ΔH. Chemical engineers use it for steam, refrigerants, distillation and vacuum drying. Only a few universities teach this inside this unit; some syllabi write Clausius–Clapeyron.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 for two-phase properties, Unit 2 for phase diagrams, and Unit 3 for latent heat.

blocks.text: At saturation, liquid and vapour coexist. The saturation curve P_sat(T) has a slope. Equality of Gibbs free energy of the two phases gives the Clapeyron equation:

blocks.where: P_sat is saturation pressure (Pa), T is absolute temperature (K), ΔH is latent heat (J/mol), and ΔV = V_g − V_l is molar volume change (m³/mol).

blocks.text: A large ΔH makes the curve steep. A large ΔV makes it flatter. For vaporisation ΔV > 0, so dP_sat/dT > 0. For ice melting, ΔV = V_liquid − V_solid < 0, so dP_sat/dT < 0: the melting point falls as pressure rises. This is why ice skates on a thin water film under pressure (see Chapter 4.3). The derivative also follows from a Maxwell relation. The equation is exact for a pure substance at coexistence; no ideal-gas assumption is used yet. ΔH is the enthalpy change from phase 1 to phase 2; its sign follows the direction. For vaporisation, ΔH is positive and the pressure rises with temperature. Use it at one temperature when ΔH and ΔV are known. It is the starting point for the ideal-vapour form below.

sections.h3: Ideal-vapour form and the straight line

blocks.text: For liquid–vapour saturation away from the critical point, V_g ≫ V_l, so ΔV ≈ V_g. Treat the vapour as ideal: V_g = RT/P_sat, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Substitution gives:

blocks.where: P_sat is saturation pressure, T is absolute temperature, ΔH is molar latent heat, and R is the gas constant.

blocks.text: Integrate from (P1, T1) to (P2, T2). For constant ΔH:

blocks.where: P1 and P2 are saturation pressures in the same unit, T1 and T2 are in K, ΔH is in J/mol, and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

blocks.text: Equivalently, ln P_sat = A − ΔH/(R T). A plot of ln P_sat against 1/T is a straight line with slope −ΔH/R. Two measured points give ΔH = −R ln(P2/P1)/(1/T2 − 1/T1). To estimate P2, use P2 = P1 exp[−(ΔH/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1)]. Convert T to kelvin and keep pressures in one unit. The figure shows water with ΔH_vap = 40.65 kJ/mol.

figure.caption: A straight line of ln P against 1/T for water. Its slope is −ΔH_vap/R; a steeper line means a larger latent heat.

spec.aria: A straight line of ln P against 1/T has slope −ΔH/R and shows how saturation pressure falls as temperature falls.

examples.question: Water has ΔH_vap = 40.65 kJ/mol and a normal boiling point of 373 K at 1 atm (101.325 kPa). Estimate its saturation pressure at 350 K using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
examples.answer: The estimated saturation pressure of water at 350 K is 42.8 kPa, about 0.428 bar.
examples.check:
import math
dH = 40650.0
R = 8.314
T1 = 373.0
T2 = 350.0
P1 = 101.325
ln_ratio = -(dH / R) * (1/T2 - 1/T1)
P2 = P1 * math.exp(ln_ratio)
print(round(ln_ratio, 4))
print(round(P2, 1))
print(round(P2 / 100, 3))

traps: Using T in °C. The equation needs kelvin; a Celsius value makes 1/T and ΔH/R(1/T2 − 1/T1) the wrong size, so the estimated pressure is badly wrong.
Dropping the minus sign in ln(P2/P1) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1).
Using V_l instead of ΔV = V_g − V_l; for vaporisation the gas volume dominates.
Mixing pressure units in P2/P1; the ratio is dimensionless, so P1 and P2 must match.
Taking the slope from P against T; −ΔH/R is the slope of ln P against 1/T.

quiz.q: State the Clapeyron equation and define ΔV.
Why is ΔV ≈ V_g valid for liquid–vapour saturation?
quiz.a: V_g is much larger than V_l away from the critical point.

quiz.q: Water: ΔH_vap = 40.65 kJ/mol, T1 = 373 K, P1 = 101.3 kPa. Estimate P_sat at 360 K.
A plot of ln P_sat against 1/T has slope −3200 K. Find ΔH_vap.
Write the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation for constant ΔH.
Why does the ideal-vapour form fail near the critical point?
quiz.a: V_l is not negligible, the vapour is not ideal, and ΔH varies.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial vapour-pressure data are often fitted with the Antoine equation, log₁₀ P = A − B/(T + C), a practical cousin of this equation. Process simulators use Wagner or DIPPR correlations near the critical point. Search "Antoine equation" and "Clausius–Clapeyron derivation" for data and practice.
